analysis.one_liner: Requires a binding code of conduct, gift disclosure, and stricter recusal rules for Supreme Court justices and federal judges.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the Supreme Court ethics bill 22–16, but the full House never voted on it and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Supreme Court and other federal courts to adopt a binding code of conduct with public notice and comment. It would have required justices to disclose gifts, income, and reimbursements; forced them off cases where a party gave them money or spent heavily to help them get their seat; and required people who fund court briefs to disclose who is paying. The House Judiciary Committee approved it 22–16, but the bill never got a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who appear in federal courts — including the Supreme Court, which currently has no enforceable ethics code — would gain from rules requiring justices to disclose gifts and income, to step aside when a party to a case funded their nomination or gave them money, and to publicly explain every disqualification. Litigants would gain the right to have a recusal decision reviewed by an outside panel of judges. The public would gain visibility into who funds the advocacy groups filing briefs at the Supreme Court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Court litigants and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue a binding code of conduct for its justices, and the Judicial Conference to do the same for lower-court judges, after public notice and comment — the Supreme Court is currently the only major American court with no adopted ethics code.
Forces justices and their law clerks to disclose gifts, reimbursements, and income under standards at least as strict as those applying to members of Congress.

Creates new automatic disqualification rules: a judge must step aside if a party to the case gave the judge or family income or gifts in the prior six years, or spent substantial funds lobbying for the judge's nomination or confirmation.

Lets litigants file a motion to disqualify a judge and have it decided by a randomly selected panel of judges from outside the case's court, with public posting of every disqualification decision and its reasons.

Requires parties and friends-of-the-court (amici) at the Supreme Court to disclose any gifts, money, or nomination-support spending they or their lawyers gave justices or their clerks, and requires outside groups filing briefs to name funders who gave more than 3% of revenue or $100,000 a year, with an annual Government Accountability Office audit.

analysis.who_pays: Supreme Court justices and federal judges, who would face enforceable disclosure and recusal obligations they currently lack. Also the companies, law firms, and advocacy groups that spend money around Supreme Court nominations and fund amicus brief campaigns, which would have to disclose those payments and gifts.

drawbacks.text: The recusal triggers are broad: a party could seek to disqualify a judge based on lobbying contacts or spending connected to the judge's nomination years earlier, which could invite tactical recusal motions that delay cases. The bill tries to manage this by requiring a good-faith certificate and affidavit and by sending contested motions to an outside panel.

The bill leaves the final check on justices with the justices themselves: when a party asks that a Supreme Court justice be disqualified, the reviewing panel is the Supreme Court (section 5(d)), so the Court still sits in judgment on its own members' conflicts.

The amicus disclosure rules would reach nonprofit and ideological groups on all sides, requiring them to name large donors (over 3% of revenue or $100,000 a year) on court briefs, which critics could argue chills association and deters small organizations from participating in major cases.

Opponents in committee could argue that judges already operate under existing federal recusal law (28 U.S.C. 455) and that a conduct code should come from the judiciary itself rather than Congress, raising a separation-of-powers objection — 16 committee members voted against reporting the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: enforceable ethics rules, gift disclosure, and outside review of recusal decisions in exchange for new paperwork and tactical-litigation risks. The transparency gains are real and targeted at a court with no enforceable code of its own. The design is not perfect — the most important weakness is that the Supreme Court itself remains the reviewing panel for disqualification motions against its own justices, and the donor-disclosure rules for amicus groups are sweeping — but on balance the bill would have imposed modest burdens on court participants in exchange for checks that do not exist today.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a 22–16 vote but House leadership never scheduled it for a floor vote, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the bill on May 3, 2022, with ten original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
On May 11, 2022, the committee held a markup session and voted 22–16 to send an amended version of the bill to the House floor.
The bill attracted 66 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The full House never took up the bill, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supreme Court justices and the parties, law firms, and advocacy groups that benefit from the current system — in which justices police their own gifts and conflicts — are better off because the bill never became law. Everyone who wanted a binding Supreme Court ethics code is no better off than before.

industries.industry: Supreme Court justices and federal judges
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the judiciary's sole control over its own ethics, imposing a binding conduct code, mandatory gift and income disclosure, automatic recusal rules, and outside review of disqualification decisions. Justices currently have no enforceable code of conduct and decide their own recusals.

industries.industry: Law firms and corporate litigants before the Supreme Court
industries.note: Repeat players at the Court — companies, their lawyers, and their officers — would have had to disclose gifts, income, and payments to justices and their clerks, and any spending supporting a justice's nomination or confirmation. Disclosure of that money would have made it harder for well-funded parties to benefit from friendly recusal decisions.

industries.industry: Advocacy groups and trade associations filing amicus briefs
industries.note: Groups that file Supreme Court and appellate briefs would have had to name funders giving more than 3% of revenue or $100,000 a year, subject to an annual GAO audit, and briefs that would force a judge's disqualification could be struck. The burden falls on all ideological sides, while the public gains visibility into who is paying to influence the Court.
